props.title: Festival Express
props.initialSlug: 1970 train tour with Grateful Dead and others

sections.content: Festival Express captures one of rock history's most legendary tours - a 1970 Canadian railway journey featuring The Grateful Dead, Janis Joplin, The Band, and other icons. Unlike Woodstock (1970) or Monterey Pop (1968), this film shows musicians in unguarded moments between shows, jamming and partying on a train. The footage sat unreleased for decades, making its 2003 emergence a time capsule of peak 1970s counterculture. Joplin's raw performances, just months before her death, are especially poignant.

sections.content: The film represents a unique moment in concert documentary style. While Monterey Pop (1968) and Jazz on a Summer's Day (1959) established the festival film format, Festival Express brings unprecedented intimacy. The train footage reveals collaborative spirit between artists who'd normally never interact this closely. We see Rick Danko and Jerry Garcia trading songs, Joplin belting blues at 3am, and Buddy Guy joining impromptu jams. This carried into their performances - the shows crackle with cross-pollination impossible at standard festivals.

The film also documents a pivotal moment in concert culture. Unlike today's corporate festivals, these shows faced protests over ticket prices ($14!). The Dead's response - playing free concerts beside the paid ones - shows how differently artists approached fan relationships then. Compare this to Stop Making Sense (1984) or Sign o' the Times (1987), where the focus shifted entirely to polished stage performances. SUBHEAD: The Lost Era of Music Documentaries

sections.content: The rediscovery and restoration of Festival Express parallels other rescued music films like Amazing Grace (2018) and Once Were Brothers (2019). This era's documentaries captured performances with minimal interference - unlike modern concert films like Justin Bieber: Never Say Never (2011) or Katy Perry: Part of Me (2012) which prioritize controlled narrative over raw footage. The unvarnished authenticity of these recovered time capsules provides crucial historical context.
